lab_title: VSEPR Theory: Mapping the Three-Dimensional Molecular World
top_level_objectives: Differentiate between electron-domain geometry and molecular geometry for molecules containing lone pairs.
Explain how electrostatic repulsion between electron domains dictates three-dimensional molecular structures.
Predict the molecular geometry and approximate bond angles of molecules containing 2 to 6 electron domains starting from their Lewis structures.
Explain why lone pairs occupy more space than bonding pairs and how this affects experimental bond angles.
Identify the preferred axial or equatorial locations of lone pairs in trigonal bipyramidal systems based on minimizing repulsive interactions.

scenes.brief_purpose: Introduce the core physical principle of VSEPR theory: that electron domains (bonds and lone pairs) around a central atom repel each other and organize themselves to maximize their mutual distance.
key_visuals: An interactive central atom anchor suspended in AR space.
Dynamic charge clouds (modeled as elastic balloons or translucent spheres) that realistically wiggle and repel each other.
A 3D angle readout display hovering above the central atom.
A 'Domain Counter' panel displaying the active number of electron domains (2 to 6).
student_actions: Use a slider to add electron domains one-by-one from 2 to 6.
Physically drag one of the domains with their hand to try and force it close to another domain, feeling haptic feedback and watching the system push back to restore the minimum-energy configuration.
Observe how the layout automatically transitions through the five basic arrangements: linear, trigonal planar, tetrahedral, trigonal bipyramidal, and octahedral.

scenes.scene_name: Tetrahedral Family and Lone Pair Repulsion
scenes.brief_purpose: Explore how the presence of lone pairs alters molecular geometry within a specific electron-domain family, focusing on the tetrahedral family (4 domains: methane, ammonia, water).
key_visuals: Side-by-side comparison models of Methane (CH4), Ammonia (NH3), and Water (H2O).
Visually distinct representations for bonding pairs (opaque cylinders with terminal atom spheres) and lone pairs (large, diffuse, glowing teardrop shapes representing high electron density).
Dynamic angle arcs displaying the bond angles: 109.5 degrees for methane, 107.3 degrees for ammonia, and 104.5 degrees for water.
student_actions: Toggle a 'Show/Hide Lone Pairs' button to see how the 'molecular geometry' only considers atomic positions, while the 'electron-domain geometry' includes the invisible lone pairs.
Rotate and inspect each model to notice how the bulky lone pairs physically crowd the bonding pairs, squeezing the hydrogen-hydrogen bonds closer together.
Classify each molecule's molecular geometry by selecting the correct term (Tetrahedral, Trigonal Pyramidal, Bent) from an AR floating menu.

scenes.scene_name: Trigonal Bipyramidal: Axial vs. Equatorial Placement
scenes.brief_purpose: Investigate the 5-domain (trigonal bipyramidal) system where positions are not equivalent, demonstrating why lone pairs preferentially occupy equatorial positions rather than axial positions to minimize 90-degree repulsions.
key_visuals: A large, interactively rotatable model of a Trigonal Bipyramidal template with color-coded axial positions (red) and equatorial positions (blue).
A 'Repulsion Stress Meter' that dynamically glows red when high-energy 90-degree interactions occur.
Real molecular models of SF4 (Seesaw) and ClF3 (T-shaped).
student_actions: Pick up a virtual 'Lone Pair' cloud and place it onto either an axial or an equatorial position on a phosphorus pentachloride template.

Observe the dynamic 'Repulsion Stress Meter' rise dramatically when a lone pair is placed axially (creating three 90-degree repulsions) versus equatorial placement (creating only two 90-degree repulsions).
Interact with the resulting Seesaw (SF4) and T-shaped (ClF3) molecules to examine how equatorial lone pair placement dictates their final real-world shapes.

scenes.scene_name: Octahedral Geometry and Square Planar Configurations
scenes.brief_purpose: Examine the 6-domain (octahedral) system to see how all positions are initially equivalent, but the introduction of a second lone pair requires 180-degree separation to minimize electrostatic repulsion.
key_visuals: An Octahedral coordinate grid template centered on a Xenon atom.
Floating models of Sulfur Hexafluoride (SF6), Bromine Pentafluoride (BrF5), and Xenon Tetrafluoride (XeF4).
Visual representation of the electrostatic field showing the symmetric distribution of negative charge when lone pairs are placed opposite one another.
student_actions: Place the first lone pair onto the octahedral central atom, observing that any of the six equivalent positions yields a square pyramidal geometry (BrF5).

Place the second lone pair onto different positions of the square pyramidal intermediate. If placed adjacent (90 degrees), watch the molecule buckle under high repulsion; if placed opposite (180 degrees), watch it stabilize into the symmetric square planar geometry (XeF4).
Confirm the structural stability by triggering an electrostatic field overlay on the finalized XeF4 molecule.

scenes.brief_purpose: Challenge students to apply their knowledge by building a 3D molecular model starting from a given 2D Lewis structure.
key_visuals: A floating digital clipboard displaying a 2D Lewis structure (e.g., Sulfur Dioxide [SO2] or Xenon Difluoride [XeF2]).
An empty central atom anchor on an interactive virtual workbench.
A 'Parts Bin' containing single bonds, double bonds, and lone pair models.
student_actions: Analyze the provided 2D Lewis structure to determine the number of bonding domains and lone pairs around the central atom.
Drag and drop the correct quantities of bonds and lone pairs from the 'Parts Bin' onto the central atom anchor.
Press a 'VSEPR Optimize' button to run the minimization simulation, watching the components rearrange in real-time into the correct 3D geometry.
Use a virtual keypad to type in or select the correct name of the resulting molecular geometry.

scenes.brief_purpose: Consolidate learning by placing all discussed molecular geometries in a virtual museum-style gallery, emphasizing real-world chemical examples and the overall predictive power of VSEPR.
key_visuals: An open-space AR gallery containing floating, rotating models of CH4, NH3, H2O, SF4, ClF3, SF6, BrF5, and XeF4.
Info placards floating beneath each molecule displaying its Lewis structure, electron-domain geometry, molecular geometry, and experimental bond angles.
An interactive 'VSEPR Periodic Table' that highlights elements and shows their common valence electron counts.
student_actions: Walk around the AR room to inspect the various molecules side-by-side.
Tap on any placard to toggle an 'Electrostatic Potential Map' overlay, illustrating how lone pairs harbor concentrated partial negative charges.
Complete a final 5-question drag-and-drop matching quiz on a floating tablet to match real molecular formulas with their corresponding VSEPR names and bond angles.
